transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I came in because I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. It’s gotten to where I sit at my kitchen table and it’s just covered—my husband’s appointment papers, church flyers, little notes from the senior center, lists I’ve started and then started again because I couldn’t find the first one… and I look at all of it and I honestly don’t know what to do first.

I’ll think, “Okay, just pick one thing,” but then one paper reminds me of another thing, and then I’m worried I’m forgetting something important, and before I know it I’ve sat there half the day. Nothing really gets done, and the pile is still there. It makes me feel awful, like I should be able to handle ordinary things better than this.
Have you been having problems with your memory?

Yes… I think so. It’s not like I don’t know who people are or anything like that, but day to day, I forget things I really meant to do. I’ve missed returning phone calls because I’ll see the message and think, “I’ll call after lunch,” and then it’s just gone from my mind until days later. Bills get tucked under a stack of mail and I don’t realize they’re still sitting there until I’m sorting through things again and feel that awful sinking feeling.

And errands, too — my daughter will ask me to pick something up or drop something off, and I truly intend to do it, I even picture myself doing it, but then the day goes along and I’ll come home and remember all at once that I never did it. And with my husband’s appointments, that’s been especially upsetting. More than once I’ve realized too late that I never confirmed one of them, even though the paper was probably right there on the table. It makes me feel embarrassed, honestly, because these aren’t complicated things, but they keep slipping through.
Do you find yourself checking things over and over, even when you know you already checked them?

I’m not sure I’d say “over and over,” no. I mean, I do look back at things sometimes because I don’t trust that I’ve kept track of them properly, but it’s not like I’m standing at the stove checking the knob ten times or anything like that.

Mostly I’ll think, “Did I already look at that paper?” or “Was that appointment written down somewhere?” and then I may go back through the pile again, but that’s more because everything feels so muddled than because I feel driven to check the same thing again and again. I don’t know if that’s what you mean. It’s more like I lose confidence in whether I actually handled it, if that makes sense.
Have you gotten lost in familiar places?

No, I don’t think so… not in the sense of truly getting lost somewhere I know. I mean, I might park somewhere and have to stand there for a minute thinking, “Now which row was I in?” or I might take a wrong turn if I’m distracted, but I can usually get myself oriented again.

I haven’t had a time where I was in my own neighborhood or at the grocery store or church and didn’t know where I was. If that’s what you mean, then no, I haven’t noticed that.
When you were a child, did you already have trouble staying organized or keeping track of things?

Yes, actually… and I don’t know why I didn’t think to mention it sooner. Even when I was a little girl, that was kind of the story with me. I remember my teachers’ comments on report cards — my mother kept some of them — and it was always something like, “She’s bright, but careless,” or “needs to pay better attention to her belongings.” That word “careless” bothered me, because I wasn’t trying to be careless.

I’d forget books at school when I needed them at home, or leave homework somewhere and then be in trouble because it looked like I just hadn’t done it. And with classwork, seatwork, whatever we called it then, I often needed the teacher to remind me to finish before I could go outside for recess. I’d start it, or mean to finish it, and then somehow I just wouldn’t be done when everyone else was lining up.

So yes… looking back, keeping track of things and staying organized was hard for me even then.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, no. I mean, I worry about things the way anybody my age probably does — if there’s something with family, or an appointment coming up, or some practical thing I need to deal with. But I don’t think I sit around worrying about lots of different things when nothing is really happening.

Sometimes I may have something on my mind longer than I should, but usually there’s at least some reason for it. So if you mean constant worry jumping from one topic to another for no clear reason, I don’t think that’s really what I experience.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?

I don’t think so, no… not most days. I mean, I have my moments, certainly. At 70, there are days where I feel a little discouraged or tired of dealing with things, or I’ll get frustrated with myself, but I wouldn’t describe it as being depressed most of the time.

It’s more like it comes and goes with circumstances. If something upsetting happens, I’ll feel down for a bit, but I don’t usually wake up day after day feeling like there’s a cloud over me, if that’s what you mean. So… no, I haven’t really noticed feeling depressed most days.
Compared with how you were for most of your adult life, have these problems with organization and forgetting gotten clearly worse in the last few years?

Yes… I would say it has gotten clearly worse, or at least it’s been causing much more trouble, over the last year or so. Maybe a little more than a year — about a year and three months, I’d say.

It really seemed to become more of a problem after my husband started needing regular help with his appointments and the daily arrangements around that. Before then, I always had some difficulty keeping things straight, but I could sort of manage it in my own way. Once there were more appointments to remember, more things to coordinate, more little details that mattered, it started to feel like I was dropping the ball much more often.

So yes, compared with most of my adult life, this last year and three months has been noticeably harder.
Because of these memory and organization problems, have you needed someone else to take over things like paying bills or managing appointments for you?

Yes… not completely take over, but my daughter has started checking behind me, which is hard to admit. She’ll ask whether a bill was paid, or she’ll look over the appointments with me, because she doesn’t really trust that I’ll keep it all straight on my own anymore. And I can’t say she’s wrong, even though it bothers me.

There was also a big event at the senior center that I used to lead, and I had to give that up. It involved too many moving pieces — times, people to call, little arrangements — and I just wasn’t managing it reliably. I felt embarrassed, because I’d done things like that before and I liked being useful, but it got to the point where I was afraid I’d miss something important.

So… yes, I guess I haven’t had someone fully take over my life, but I do need more oversight now than I used to.
Have you had trouble finding the right words when you’re speaking?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean… everyone has moments where a word is on the tip of their tongue, don’t they? I’ll sometimes pause and say, “Oh, what’s that called again?” but I don’t know that it’s been something I’d point to as a real problem.

I haven’t noticed myself regularly using the wrong words or being unable to get a sentence out. At least, no one has really said to me, “You’re having trouble talking,” or anything like that. It’s more just the ordinary kind of searching for a name or a word now and then, as far as I can tell.

So… I don’t think so, not in any major way.
Do you have more trouble learning new information now than you used to?

I’m not really sure how to answer that. I don’t think I’ve noticed a clear change where I’d say, “Oh, I can’t learn things anymore,” if that’s what you mean. It’s more that if someone tells me something new, I may need it repeated, or I may want to write it down, but I don’t know if that’s learning exactly or just me not keeping it in my head the first time.

If it’s something I’m interested in and I can take my time with it, I think I can still pick it up. But if someone explains something quickly, especially with a lot of steps, I can get a little overwhelmed and then I’m not sure I absorbed it properly. I wouldn’t say I’ve sat down and tested myself, though, so it’s hard for me to compare.

So… maybe a little, but I can’t say for certain that learning new information itself is worse. I just notice I need more time and reminders than I used to.
Do you often forget conversations or events that happened just a short time earlier, even after someone has already told you them?

I don’t know that I’d say I “often” forget whole conversations or events right after they happen. I mean, there are times when someone will say, “I told you that,” and I’ll have this awful feeling because I truly don’t remember the moment they said it, or I only remember it once they give me a lot of hints. But I’m not sure how often is often, if that makes sense.

Sometimes I think maybe I wasn’t fully paying attention when they told me, so then later it looks like I forgot, but maybe I never really took it in properly in the first place. Like if someone tells me something while I’m doing something else, or if there are a lot of little details, then yes, I may need them to tell me again. But if it’s a big event or a real conversation where I’m sitting there focused, I usually have some sense of it afterward.

So… I guess I do have moments like that, and they bother me, but I’m not sure I can say I’m forgetting entire recent conversations all the time. It’s more uneven than that.
Do you find that you forget things you were just told even when you were paying close attention at the time?

I’m not completely sure. If I’m truly paying close attention — like I’m looking at the person, I’m not trying to do something else, and I know I need to remember what they’re saying — I usually feel like I’ve got it in the moment. But then later, sometimes it’s fuzzier than I expected, and I’ll think, “Wait, did they say Tuesday or Thursday?” or “Was I supposed to call them, or were they calling me?” So I don’t know if that counts as forgetting what I was just told, or if it’s more that the details don’t stick very well.

It’s hard because I can feel like I’m listening. I’m nodding, I’m following along, I may even repeat it back in my head. But then afterward, unless I wrote it down or there’s something to remind me, some part of it may just sort of… slip away. Not always, and I don’t want to make it sound like every conversation disappears, because it doesn’t. But yes, there are times when I’m surprised by how little stayed with me, even though I thought I was paying attention.
Have family members or friends told you that your thinking or memory has clearly changed from how you used to be?

I don’t think anyone has said it in that clear a way, like, “Your thinking has changed,” or “Your memory is worse than it used to be.” Not that I can remember, anyway. People close to me may get frustrated if I ask something again or if I don’t keep track of what was said, but I don’t know that they’ve described it as a definite change.

That’s part of what makes it hard for me to answer, because I’m not always the best judge of what other people are noticing. Sometimes I wonder if they just think I’m distracted, or not listening closely enough, rather than thinking my memory itself has changed. And I suppose if someone did say something casually, I might not have taken it as a serious comment.

But no, I can’t say family or friends have clearly told me that I’m different from how I used to be in that way. If they have concerns, they haven’t really sat me down and said it plainly.
Before this last year, were you able to manage your bills and appointments on your own without anyone checking behind you?

Before this last year… I think I was managing more of it myself, yes. I mean, I’ve always had my little systems — notes on the calendar, piles of papers that probably only made sense to me — but I did handle my own bills and appointments without someone standing over me.

Now it’s different, and I don’t like admitting that. My daughter has started checking behind me with bills and appointments, not every single second, but enough that it’s clear she doesn’t really trust me to keep it all straight on my own anymore. She’ll ask, “Did you pay that?” or “Are you sure that appointment is this week?” and sometimes she’ll look at the statements or the calendar herself.

And I also had to step back from leading this big event at the senior center, which was really upsetting. I used to be able to organize things like that and keep track of the moving parts, but it got to where it was too much, and I couldn’t reliably stay on top of it. So, yes, before this past year I was more independent with those things, and now I do need someone checking behind me more than I used to.
When you write information down right away, are you usually able to remember it later?

If I write it down right away, it helps, but I can’t honestly say that means I always remember it later. Sometimes the note works only if I actually see it again at the right time, you know? Like, I’ll write something on a scrap of paper or put it in a notebook, and then the paper gets buried under mail or the notebook isn’t open, and it’s almost like I never wrote it down at all.

That’s happened with everyday things. I’ve missed returning phone calls even when I meant to call back, and I’ve left bills sitting under a stack of mail because I wrote something down or set it aside and then it just disappeared from my mind. I’ve also forgotten errands I promised my daughter I’d do, which makes me feel awful because I really do intend to help her. And more than once I realized too late that I never confirmed one of my husband’s appointments, even though I thought I had made myself some kind of reminder.

So writing it down helps some, yes, but it’s not enough by itself. If the note isn’t somewhere obvious, or if I don’t check it at the right moment, it doesn’t reliably come back to me.
Has your daughter told you that your memory or thinking is clearly worse than it used to be?

I’m not sure she’s said it in those exact words, no. She’ll point things out, and sometimes she sounds worried or frustrated, but I don’t remember her sitting me down and saying, “Your memory is clearly worse,” or “Your thinking has changed.” 

It’s more indirect than that, I think. She’ll ask questions or double-check things, and I can tell she’s concerned, but I don’t want to put words in her mouth. Maybe she thinks it, I don’t know. But if you’re asking whether she has plainly told me that I’m worse than I used to be, I don’t think so — not that directly.
Has anyone close to you clearly said that your memory or thinking has gotten worse than it used to be?

I don’t think anyone has said it that clearly, no. At least, not in a way I can point to and say, yes, they told me my memory or thinking is worse than it used to be.

People close to me might ask questions or repeat things, and I can sometimes feel that they’re watching a little more closely, but that’s different from someone actually saying, “You’ve gotten worse.” I don’t want to exaggerate or put words in anyone’s mouth. If someone has hinted at it, maybe I didn’t take it that way at the time, but I can’t honestly say anyone close to me has clearly said that to me.
Have you been diagnosed with any medical or neurological illness that you think might be affecting your memory or thinking?

Not that I can think of, no. I mean, I’ve had the usual things you collect by this age, and I’ve seen doctors for this and that, but I don’t believe anyone has diagnosed me with a medical or neurological illness and said, “This is why your memory or thinking is affected.”

I’m trying to be careful because sometimes I don’t know what counts as neurological, exactly. If you mean something like a condition of the brain or nerves that a doctor specifically identified, then no, I don’t think I’ve been told that. At least nothing comes to mind that I would connect directly to my memory or thinking.
Has your daughter clearly noticed that your memory or thinking has changed from how you used to be?

I’m not really sure. I mean, she may have noticed things here and there, because she does ask me about things sometimes, or she’ll check what I meant, that sort of thing. But I don’t know that she has clearly said, “Mom, you’ve changed,” or made it that definite.

It’s hard for me to separate what she’s actually noticed from what I think she might be thinking, if that makes sense. Sometimes I read into her tone, and then I wonder if I’m making too much of it. So I can’t honestly say yes, she has clearly noticed a change from how I used to be. She might have concerns, but I don’t know that for certain.

patient.answer:

patient.answer:
Yes… I would say it has gotten clearly worse, or at least it’s been causing much more trouble, over the last year or so. Maybe a little more than a year — about a year and three months, I’d say.

It really seemed to become more of a problem after my husband started needing regular help with his appointments and the daily arrangements around that. Before then, I always had some difficulty keeping things straight, but I could sort of manage it in my own way. Once there were more appointments to remember, more things to coordinate, more little details that mattered, it started to feel like I was dropping the ball much more often.

So yes, compared with most of my adult life, this last year and three months has been noticeably harder.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a decline in instrumental activities of daily living due to cognitive problems, which would favor an unspecified neurocognitive disorder over lifelong ADHD with recent increased demands.
doctor.question: Because of these memory and organization problems, have you needed someone else to take over things like paying bills or managing appointments for you?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I had to give up leading a big senior-center event, and my daughter has started double-checking bills and appointments because she no longer trusts that I can keep everything straight on my own.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the memory and organization problems have caused real-life impairment requiring someone else to help manage bills or appointments.

patient.answer:
Yes… not completely take over, but my daughter has started checking behind me, which is hard to admit. She’ll ask whether a bill was paid, or she’ll look over the appointments with me, because she doesn’t really trust that I’ll keep it all straight on my own anymore. And I can’t say she’s wrong, even though it bothers me.

There was also a big event at the senior center that I used to lead, and I had to give that up. It involved too many moving pieces — times, people to call, little arrangements — and I just wasn’t managing it reliably. I felt embarrassed, because I’d done things like that before and I liked being useful, but it got to the point where I was afraid I’d miss something important.

So… yes, I guess I haven’t had someone fully take over my life, but I do need more oversight now than I used to.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a decline in other cognitive abilities besides attention/organization, which would support a neurocognitive disorder over lifelong ADHD.
doctor.question: Have you had trouble finding the right words when you’re speaking?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about word-finding or language difficulty, which is not covered by the listed ADHD symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure, honestly. I mean… everyone has moments where a word is on the tip of their tongue, don’t they? I’ll sometimes pause and say, “Oh, what’s that called again?” but I don’t know that it’s been something I’d point to as a real problem.

I haven’t noticed myself regularly using the wrong words or being unable to get a sentence out. At least, no one has really said to me, “You’re having trouble talking,” or anything like that. It’s more just the ordinary kind of searching for a name or a word now and then, as far as I can tell.

So… I don’t think so, not in any major way.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a clear decline from her longstanding baseline in learning/retaining new information, which would help distinguish lifelong ADHD from a neurocognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Do you have more trouble learning new information now than you used to?

target_item.reason: The question is about difficulty learning new information compared with before, which is not directly covered by the listed ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that. I don’t think I’ve noticed a clear change where I’d say, “Oh, I can’t learn things anymore,” if that’s what you mean. It’s more that if someone tells me something new, I may need it repeated, or I may want to write it down, but I don’t know if that’s learning exactly or just me not keeping it in my head the first time.

If it’s something I’m interested in and I can take my time with it, I think I can still pick it up. But if someone explains something quickly, especially with a lot of steps, I can get a little overwhelmed and then I’m not sure I absorbed it properly. I wouldn’t say I’ve sat down and tested myself, though, so it’s hard for me to compare.

So… maybe a little, but I can’t say for certain that learning new information itself is worse. I just notice I need more time and reminders than I used to.

doctor.intent: Differentiate lifelong ADHD with recent increased demands from a neurocognitive disorder by testing for impaired retention of recently learned information.
doctor.question: Do you often forget conversations or events that happened just a short time earlier, even after someone has already told you them?

target_item.reason: The question is about short-term episodic memory, such as forgetting recent conversations or events even after being told; the provided symptom profile covers ADHD-related forgetfulness in daily activities, not this specific memory problem.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d say I “often” forget whole conversations or events right after they happen. I mean, there are times when someone will say, “I told you that,” and I’ll have this awful feeling because I truly don’t remember the moment they said it, or I only remember it once they give me a lot of hints. But I’m not sure how often is often, if that makes sense.

Sometimes I think maybe I wasn’t fully paying attention when they told me, so then later it looks like I forgot, but maybe I never really took it in properly in the first place. Like if someone tells me something while I’m doing something else, or if there are a lot of little details, then yes, I may need them to tell me again. But if it’s a big event or a real conversation where I’m sitting there focused, I usually have some sense of it afterward.

So… I guess I do have moments like that, and they bother me, but I’m not sure I can say I’m forgetting entire recent conversations all the time. It’s more uneven than that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is clear impairment in delayed recall of recently learned information, which would favor a neurocognitive disorder over lifelong ADHD-related inattention.
doctor.question: Do you find that you forget things you were just told even when you were paying close attention at the time?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about immediate forgetting of information despite paying close attention, which points more to a memory/learning problem than to any listed ADHD symptom profile. The available profiles cover forgetfulness in daily activities, distractibility, losing items, and organization issues, but not this kind of short-term memory failure when attention was intact.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure. If I’m truly paying close attention — like I’m looking at the person, I’m not trying to do something else, and I know I need to remember what they’re saying — I usually feel like I’ve got it in the moment. But then later, sometimes it’s fuzzier than I expected, and I’ll think, “Wait, did they say Tuesday or Thursday?” or “Was I supposed to call them, or were they calling me?” So I don’t know if that counts as forgetting what I was just told, or if it’s more that the details don’t stick very well.

It’s hard because I can feel like I’m listening. I’m nodding, I’m following along, I may even repeat it back in my head. But then afterward, unless I wrote it down or there’s something to remind me, some part of it may just sort of… slip away. Not always, and I don’t want to make it sound like every conversation disappears, because it doesn’t. But yes, there are times when I’m surprised by how little stayed with me, even though I thought I was paying attention.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective evidence of broad cognitive decline beyond lifelong attentional/executive problems, which would favor F09 over ADHD.
doctor.question: Have family members or friends told you that your thinking or memory has clearly changed from how you used to be?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether family or friends have observed a clear change in thinking or memory compared with before, which is not directly covered by the listed ADHD symptom items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think anyone has said it in that clear a way, like, “Your thinking has changed,” or “Your memory is worse than it used to be.” Not that I can remember, anyway. People close to me may get frustrated if I ask something again or if I don’t keep track of what was said, but I don’t know that they’ve described it as a definite change.

That’s part of what makes it hard for me to answer, because I’m not always the best judge of what other people are noticing. Sometimes I wonder if they just think I’m distracted, or not listening closely enough, rather than thinking my memory itself has changed. And I suppose if someone did say something casually, I might not have taken it as a serious comment.

But no, I can’t say family or friends have clearly told me that I’m different from how I used to be in that way. If they have concerns, they haven’t really sat me down and said it plainly.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a clear decline in basic instrumental functioning from the patient’s lifelong baseline, which would favor a neurocognitive disorder over ADHD.
doctor.question: Before this last year, were you able to manage your bills and appointments on your own without anyone checking behind you?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I had to give up leading a big senior-center event, and my daughter has started double-checking bills and appointments because she no longer trusts that I can keep everything straight on my own.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether problems with bills and appointments have affected independent functioning and led to someone checking behind her.

patient.answer:
Before this last year… I think I was managing more of it myself, yes. I mean, I’ve always had my little systems — notes on the calendar, piles of papers that probably only made sense to me — but I did handle my own bills and appointments without someone standing over me.

Now it’s different, and I don’t like admitting that. My daughter has started checking behind me with bills and appointments, not every single second, but enough that it’s clear she doesn’t really trust me to keep it all straight on my own anymore. She’ll ask, “Did you pay that?” or “Are you sure that appointment is this week?” and sometimes she’ll look at the statements or the calendar herself.

And I also had to step back from leading this big event at the senior center, which was really upsetting. I used to be able to organize things like that and keep track of the moving parts, but it got to where it was too much, and I couldn’t reliably stay on top of it. So, yes, before this past year I was more independent with those things, and now I do need someone checking behind me more than I used to.

inference.note: Worsening over the last ~15 months with decline from prior baseline and new need for oversight in bills/appointments suggests acquired cognitive disorder in addition to lifelong inattentive symptoms. Added F06.7 for mild neurocognitive disorder; retained F09 because etiology is still unspecified.

doctor.intent: Distinguish long-standing ADHD with situational worsening from a neurocognitive disorder by testing whether attention-related memory failures improve when information is externally encoded.
doctor.question: When you write information down right away, are you usually able to remember it later?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: I’ve missed returning calls, left bills sitting under a stack of mail, forgotten errands I promised my daughter I’d do, and more than once realized too late that I never confirmed one of my husband’s appointments.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether writing information down helps me remember it later, which most directly relates to forgetfulness in daily activities such as keeping appointments, returning calls, and managing bills.

patient.answer:
If I write it down right away, it helps, but I can’t honestly say that means I always remember it later. Sometimes the note works only if I actually see it again at the right time, you know? Like, I’ll write something on a scrap of paper or put it in a notebook, and then the paper gets buried under mail or the notebook isn’t open, and it’s almost like I never wrote it down at all.

That’s happened with everyday things. I’ve missed returning phone calls even when I meant to call back, and I’ve left bills sitting under a stack of mail because I wrote something down or set it aside and then it just disappeared from my mind. I’ve also forgotten errands I promised my daughter I’d do, which makes me feel awful because I really do intend to help her. And more than once I realized too late that I never confirmed one of my husband’s appointments, even though I thought I had made myself some kind of reminder.

So writing it down helps some, yes, but it’s not enough by itself. If the note isn’t somewhere obvious, or if I don’t check it at the right moment, it doesn’t reliably come back to me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective evidence of cognitive decline from a knowledgeable informant, which best distinguishes mild neurocognitive disorder from longstanding ADHD or unspecified cognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Has your daughter told you that your memory or thinking is clearly worse than it used to be?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether the daughter has observed a clear worsening in memory or thinking compared with before, which is about cognitive change reported by an informant rather than any listed ADHD symptom profile item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure she’s said it in those exact words, no. She’ll point things out, and sometimes she sounds worried or frustrated, but I don’t remember her sitting me down and saying, “Your memory is clearly worse,” or “Your thinking has changed.” 

It’s more indirect than that, I think. She’ll ask questions or double-check things, and I can tell she’s concerned, but I don’t want to put words in her mouth. Maybe she thinks it, I don’t know. But if you’re asking whether she has plainly told me that I’m worse than I used to be, I don’t think so — not that directly.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective corroboration of a clear decline from prior functioning, which best separates mild neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition from longstanding ADHD or unspecified cognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Has anyone close to you clearly said that your memory or thinking has gotten worse than it used to be?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether someone close has clearly observed a worsening in memory or thinking compared with before, which is about collateral report of cognitive decline rather than any listed ADHD symptom profile item.

patient.answer:
I don’t think anyone has said it that clearly, no. At least, not in a way I can point to and say, yes, they told me my memory or thinking is worse than it used to be.

People close to me might ask questions or repeat things, and I can sometimes feel that they’re watching a little more closely, but that’s different from someone actually saying, “You’ve gotten worse.” I don’t want to exaggerate or put words in anyone’s mouth. If someone has hinted at it, maybe I didn’t take it that way at the time, but I can’t honestly say anyone close to me has clearly said that to me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a clear medical or neurological cause for the recent cognitive worsening, which would favor mild neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition (F06.7) or unspecified mental disorder due to known physiological condition (F09) over lifelong ADHD with age-related strain.
doctor.question: Have you been diagnosed with any medical or neurological illness that you think might be affecting your memory or thinking?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about diagnosed medical or neurological illnesses that could affect memory or thinking, which is not covered by the listed ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Not that I can think of, no. I mean, I’ve had the usual things you collect by this age, and I’ve seen doctors for this and that, but I don’t believe anyone has diagnosed me with a medical or neurological illness and said, “This is why your memory or thinking is affected.”

I’m trying to be careful because sometimes I don’t know what counts as neurological, exactly. If you mean something like a condition of the brain or nerves that a doctor specifically identified, then no, I don’t think I’ve been told that. At least nothing comes to mind that I would connect directly to my memory or thinking.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective evidence of cognitive decline from a knowledgeable informant, which would distinguish mild neurocognitive disorder from ADHD or unspecified neurocognitive disorder.
doctor.question: Has your daughter clearly noticed that your memory or thinking has changed from how you used to be?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether the daughter has clearly noticed a change in memory or thinking from baseline, which is about observed cognitive decline rather than any listed ADHD symptom or requirement.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I mean, she may have noticed things here and there, because she does ask me about things sometimes, or she’ll check what I meant, that sort of thing. But I don’t know that she has clearly said, “Mom, you’ve changed,” or made it that definite.

It’s hard for me to separate what she’s actually noticed from what I think she might be thinking, if that makes sense. Sometimes I read into her tone, and then I wonder if I’m making too much of it. So I can’t honestly say yes, she has clearly noticed a change from how I used to be. She might have concerns, but I don’t know that for certain.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient’s main reason for seeking help today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a longstanding history since childhood of disorganization and inattentive-type symptoms, but also reports a clear recent worsening over the last approximately 15 months with increased forgetting and decline from prior adult functioning, now requiring oversight for bills and appointments and relinquishing a complex community role. This pattern is more consistent with mild cognitive disorder superimposed on lifelong attentional weaknesses than with ADHD alone. Full dementia/unspecified organic mental disorder is less supported because she remains largely independent, is not getting lost in familiar places, and has no major language impairment.
